text: Clinic follow-up, 60-year-old female here for blood pressure management. She reports home readings averaging 155/95 despite adherence to lisinopril 20 mg daily. Denies chest pain, headache, or visual changes. Exam: BP 158/96 in left arm, HR 78 regular, lungs clear, no edema, fundi show mild arteriolar narrowing. Basic metabolic panel and urinalysis unremarkable; ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no LVH strain. Assessment: essential hypertension, inadequately controlled on monotherapy. Plan: increase lisinopril to 40 mg daily and add hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, encourage low-sodium diet, recheck BP and repeat basic metabolic panel in 4 weeks, continue home BP log.

60-year-old male presenting to weight management clinic. BMI 29.4, weight up 6 lb since last visit. He also reports lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, forgetfulness, distractibility, and impulsive task-switching that has worsened since retirement; adult ADHD screening (ASRS) strongly positive. Exam unremarkable aside from increased abdominal girth. Plan: nutrition counseling and structured activity program targeting 5-7% weight loss; start extended-release methylphenidate 20 mg daily for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with follow-up in six weeks to assess symptom control and appetite effects.

Inpatient progress note: 45-year-old male admitted with dyspnea and hypoxia; CT angiogram showed segmental pulmonary embolism, and he is on heparin infusion. He has been anemic for months with fatigue and pallor; hemoglobin today 8.9 g/dL with low normal indices, workup to date unrevealing, treated as unspecified anemia with iron supplementation. Overnight he developed rhinorrhea, sore throat, and cough without fever, exam with clear lungs, consistent with an acute upper respiratory infection; supportive care only. Plan: transition to oral anticoagulation, continue iron, hematologic workup pending, symptom relief with fluids and acetaminophen, monitor oxygen saturation.

54F seen in pulmonary clinic for wheezing, nocturnal cough, and shortness of breath triggered by cold air and respiratory infections. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.65 with 14% bronchodilator reversibility, confirming asthma. Currently using albuterol rescue inhaler more than 3 times weekly; nighttime awakenings twice monthly — moderate persistent asthma. No emergency visits this year. Exam: expiratory wheezes bilaterally, otherwise normal. Plan: start inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta agonist combination, update asthma action plan, review inhaler technique, prescribe spacer, annual flu vaccine and pneumococcal immunization, follow-up spirometry in 6 weeks, return immediately with worsening symptoms.

Neurology clinic. 56-year-old male with long-standing epilepsy, characterized by generalized tonic-clonic seizures since age 30, currently about one breakthrough seizure every two months despite levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Exam nonfocal; EEG shows interictal epileptiform discharges. He also reports progressive urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia twice nightly over the past year; prostate exam reveals a smoothly enlarged gland, and post-void residual is 90 mL, consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Plan: add lamotrigine taper; start tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly; check PSA; urology referral if symptoms persist; no driving until seizure-free.

ED note. 23-year-old man brought in by ambulance with acute right-sided weakness and slurred speech onset ~2 hours ago. Head CT shows hypoattenuation in the left MCA territory consistent with acute ischemic infarction; thrombolysis administered after screening. History significant for heavy alcohol use — roughly a pint of spirits daily for five years, prior withdrawal seizure, elevated GGT and macrocytosis on labs, meeting criteria for alcohol use disorder. He reports morning shakes relieved by drinking and failed prior attempts to stop. Exam: right hemiparesis 3/5, right facial droop, dysarthria. Plan: admit to stroke unit, repeat imaging, physical therapy evaluation; thiamine and folate; alcohol withdrawal protocol with lorazepam PRN; addiction medicine consult for relapse prevention and detoxification planning prior to discharge.

Hospital ward note, Rheumatology consult. 84-year-old man admitted with 24 hours of exquisite pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth of the first right metatarsophalangeal joint, unable to ambulate; he had a similar episode two years ago involving the left ankle. Serum uric acid 9.2 mg/dL. Joint aspiration deferred given classic presentation and comorbidities; clinical diagnosis of acute gout flare. Started on colchicine with rapid improvement; prednisone taper considered but held given response. Discussion of chronic urate-lowering therapy with allopuricil to begin after flare resolution, target uric acid below 6. Discharge planning: home, podiatry referral, dietary counseling regarding purine intake and alcohol moderation, rheumatology follow-up in 4 weeks.

Primary care clinic. 53-year-old male presents for bone health follow-up. DEXA scan shows osteoporosis with T-score of -2.8 at the lumbar spine and -2.5 at the femoral neck, without any fracture history or compression deformity; started on alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. His BMI is 32, falling in the obese range; weight-loss plan discussed with dietitian referral and exercise program. No steroid use. Exam unremarkable, no kyphosis or spinal tenderness. Plan: repeat DEXA in 2 years, fall prevention counseling, alendronate administration instructions reviewed, weight recheck at next visit.

Urgent care visit. 87-year-old male with 4 days of thick nasal discharge, facial pressure over the cheeks, postnasal drip, and low-grade malaise; no fever today. Exam: turbinate edema, purulent drainage bilaterally, tenderness over maxillary sinuses. Impression: acute bacterial sinusitis; started on amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 twice daily for 10 days with saline irrigation. He also carries a longstanding attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosis, historically managed with stimulant therapy; currently reports good attention with low-dose methylphenidate, no interval concerns. No allergies. Follow-up if symptoms persist beyond 10 days or worsen.

Urgent care visit. 56-year-old male with two-day sore throat, painful swallowing, and low-grade fever. No cough, no rhinorrhea. Exam: temperature 37.9 C, pharynx erythematous with tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, Centor score 3, rapid strep positive. Diagnosis: acute pharyngitis, streptococcal. Prescribed penicillin VK for ten days, gargles, and analgesics; instructed on completion of full course and return precautions for difficulty breathing or inability to tolerate liquids. Work note provided. Patient otherwise well, no chronic conditions. Follow-up only if symptoms persist beyond five days of therapy.

Urgent care clinic. 26-year-old male with recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia, nausea, and visual aura lasting 4-6 hours, occurring several times monthly — consistent with migraine. He also has a three-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis affecting his wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints, currently on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and adalimumab; mild synovitis noted bilaterally. Today he also reports dysuria and urgency for two days; urinalysis shows pyuria, positive nitrites, and leukocyte esterase — a urinary tract infection. Plan: sumatriptan as needed for migraines with prophylaxis considered if frequency increases, continue RA regimen with rheumatology follow-up, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the UTI with increased fluids.

ED note. 35-year-old man with long-standing ADHD on methylphenidate presents with 18 hours of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, and nausea. He also reports a chronic eczematous rash on his flexor forearms, currently flaring. Exam: T 100.8 F, McBurney point tenderness with guarding, positive Rovsing sign; scaly, erythematous, lichenified plaques on antecubital folds. Labs: WBC 15.2 with left shift. CT abdomen: dilated appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding, no perforation. Assessment: acute appendicitis; ADHD, medications continued; atopic dermatitis flare. Plan: admitted to surgery, laparoscopic appendectomy tonight; resume stimulant postoperatively; triamcinolone 0.1% cream to flexor areas.

35F telehealth visit for cognitive and movement concerns. Established diagnoses of Parkinson disease (diagnosed age 32, on carbidopa/levodopa, resting tremor right hand, bradykinesia) and early-onset Alzheimer disease (progressive short-term memory loss, MoCA 21/30, on donepezil). Also with chronic dorsalgia across the lower back, worsened by prolonged sitting. Repeat lipid panel today shows LDL 190 mg/dL, total cholesterol 280, consistent with her familial hyperlipidemia; she remains on atorvastatin. Plan: adjust statin dose, physical therapy referral for back pain and gentle stretching program, continue neurology follow-up for both neurodegenerative conditions, repeat lipids in 3 months.

Hospital ward admission. 33-year-old male with type 2 diabetes on metformin and semaglutide presents with two days of diffuse abdominal and pelvic pain, nausea, and palpitations. ECG shows irregularly irregular rhythm without delta waves — atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Exam: JVD, bibasilar crackles, mild hepatomegaly; BNP elevated, troponin negative. Echocardiogram: reduced ejection fraction consistent with heart failure. Abdominal pain attributed to hepatic congestion; CT unremarkable otherwise. Started on IV diltiazem then transitioned to oral, furosemide with good diuresis, continued metformin, insulin sliding scale in hospital. Pain resolving with decongestion. Plan: anticoagulation discussion, cardiology follow-up, repeat echo in six weeks.

General surgery clinic. 50-year-old female evaluated for right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, radiating to the right shoulder, with nausea. Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrates multiple gallstones with a 4 mm stone, gallbladder wall not thickened, no periductal dilation — cholelithiasis. Plan: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, low-fat diet until surgery. Incidentally, she reports nocturia, weak urinary stream, hesitancy, and incomplete emptying; examination and post-void residual of 120 mL support bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Urology consultation arranged; initiated tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly with symptom reassessment in four weeks.

Clinic visit. 24-year-old female with several days of diffuse myalgias, low-grade fever, sore throat, and nasal congestion — consistent with a viral illness; no focal findings, negative rapid strep. Also here for flare of her psoriasis: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale over extensor surfaces of elbows and knees, roughly 8% BSA, mildly pruritic. Currently using intermittent topical steroid. Plan: supportive care with fluids, acetaminophen as needed for viral symptoms; continue clobetasol 0.05% ointment BID to plaques for two weeks, add moisturizer. Dermatology follow-up in six weeks; return sooner if fevers persist beyond five days.

Behavioral health clinic, follow-up visit. 60-year-old female presents with six weeks of persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep with early morning awakening, decreased appetite, and difficulty concentrating at work. She denies any prior episodes of depression or manic symptoms; this is her first episode. PHQ-9 score 18. Denies suicidal ideation. Exam: flat affect, psychomotor slowing, otherwise unremarkable. Plan: started sertraline 50 mg daily, referred for cognitive behavioral therapy, follow-up in four weeks. Encourated daily walking and sleep hygiene.

Internal medicine clinic. 62-year-old male for follow-up of multiple chronic issues. Blood pressure today 152/94, averaging 150/90 on home readings; essential hypertension confirmed, lisinopril increased from 20 to 40 mg daily. Recent right upper quadrant ultrasound showed diffuse hepatic steatosis with normal liver size, consistent with fatty liver disease; LFTs mildly elevated (ALT 68, AST 52); advised weight reduction and alcohol abstinence. Also reports symmetric morning stiffness lasting over an hour in both hands, wrists, and MCP joints with swelling and tenderness; RF positive and anti-CCP positive, consistent with rheumatoid arthritis; referred to rheumatology, started on naproxen 500 mg twice daily with PPI cover while awaiting appointment. Repeat metabolic panel and BP check in six weeks.

Clinic visit. 32-year-old male with long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes presents with two weeks of epigastric burning, nausea after meals, and occasional coffee-ground emesis. Has had T1DM since age 14; uses an insulin pump, checks glucose 6 times daily; recent A1c 7.4%. Denies NSAID use but admits heavy alcohol on weekends. Exam: mild epigastric tenderness without rebound, no organomegaly. Stool guaiac trace positive. Plan: continue basal-bolus insulin via pump; start omeprazole 40 mg daily, avoid alcohol and NSAIDs; H. pylori serology sent; repeat hemoglobin and hematocrit in 2 weeks; GI referral for EGD if symptoms persist. Follow-up in 4 weeks with fasting glucose log.

Telehealth visit. 87-year-old male with three days of sore throat, nasal congestion, and dry cough, no fever; exam via video unremarkable, diagnosis acute upper respiratory infection, supportive care advised, no antibiotics. Chronic kidney disease stage 3 with baseline creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, eGFR 38; labs today stable, continue current regimen, avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxics. BMI 30.4, obesity documented; nutritionist follow-up for weight management reiterated. Reviewed home medications; no changes needed. Patient instructed to seek in-person care for fever, worsening dyspnea, or decreased urine output. Follow-up telehealth visit in two weeks to recheck symptoms and renal function with lab draw at local facility.

Telehealth visit, neurology follow-up. 76-year-old female with recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea, consistent with her migraine history; she reports 3 attacks this month, partially relieved by sumatriptan. She also endorses daytime somnolence, loud snoring, and witnessed pauses in breathing overnight; prior sleep study confirmed obstructive sleep apnea, and she is adherent to CPAP. Intermittent wheezing and shortness of breath with exertion persist; she uses albuterol and fluticasone-salmeterol for her asthma, with no nighttime flares this month. Plan: continue triptan with addition of topiramate for prophylaxis, reinforce CPAP compliance, review inhaler technique, and schedule pulmonary function testing. Return sooner for chest pain or severe headache change.

Clinic visit. 47-year-old male presents with 6 weeks of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, and 8-lb weight loss despite good appetite. Exam: HR 112, mild lid lag, smooth diffuse goiter, fine tremor of outstretched hands. TSH <0.01, free T4 elevated; started on methimazole and propranolol. Also reports recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea, consistent with migraines; will continue sumatriptan PRN. Additionally, 5 days of facial pressure over maxillary region, purulent nasal discharge, and congestion consistent with acute bacterial sinusitis; started amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days and saline rinses. Recheck thyroid panel in 4 weeks. Return sooner if symptoms worsen.

Cardiology clinic. 69-year-old male with chronic heart failure, reduced ejection fraction of 30% on last echocardiogram, presents with increasing exertional dyspnea and orthopnea over the past week. Exam: elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, S3 gallop, trace lower extremity edema, weight up 4 pounds. Currently on sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone, and dapagliflozin. Labs: BNP elevated at 850. No chest pain. Plan: increase furosemide to 80 mg daily, strict daily weights and sodium restriction, reassess in 2 weeks, repeat BMP, consider ICD discussion given persistent low EF.

Clinic SOAP: 58-year-old transgender female (assigned male at birth, on estrogen therapy) presents with fatigue. Labs show hemoglobin 9.8, MCV 71, ferritin 6 — iron deficiency anemia; oral iron started and colonoscopy scheduled. Chronic irregular bowel habits with alternating loose stools and constipation, bloating relieved by defecation, no alarm features — irritable bowel syndrome managed with diet and antispasmodics. Extensor surface plaques with silvery scale on elbows and knees, stable psoriasis; continuing topical corticosteroid and vitamin D analog. She also reports weakened urinary stream, nocturia twice nightly, and incomplete emptying; exam and prior ultrasound confirm benign prostatic hyperplasia; tamsulosin initiated. Plan: repeat CBC in 8 weeks, GI and urology follow-up.

Neurology clinic. 68-year-old female with Parkinson disease (on carbidopa-levodopa, tremor-predominant, Hoehn & Yahr stage 2) and epilepsy on levetiracetam, seizure-free for two years, presents for follow-up. She also reports longstanding excessive worry, restlessness, and recent panic episodes with chest tightness, worse as her tremor has progressed. ECG today confirms atrial fibrillation; she is already anticoagulated with apixaban and rate-controlled on metoprolol. Exam: bilateral rest tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity; no seizure activity. Plan: add low-dose escitalopram for generalized anxiety with panic, CBT referral, continue current Parkinson and antiepileptic regimens, repeat ECG and TSH, follow up in eight weeks.

Primary care clinic. 37-year-old female seen for fatigue and routine labs. BMI 28.4 — overweight range on today's measurement. Screening labs notable for 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 14 ng/mL, consistent with deficiency; calcium, PTH, and CBC otherwise normal. No other symptoms; exam unremarkable. Plan: cholecalciferol 50,000 IU weekly for eight weeks then 1,000 IU daily maintenance, repeat level in three months. Discussed diet and physical activity; nutrition referral offered for weight management, goal of 5-10% weight reduction. Follow-up visit in three months to recheck vitamin D and weight.

Vascular clinic, 71-year-old male with bilateral calf cramping on walking two blocks, relieved by rest, plus chronic leg discoloration. Exam: absent posterior tibial pulses, cool feet, thin shiny skin, mild dependent rubor. ABI 0.7 right, 0.75 left. No ulcers or gangrene. Findings consistent with peripheral vascular disease beyond isolated claudication. Advised supervised walking program, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, statin therapy initiated. Smoking cessation counseling given. Repeat ABI and follow-up in 3 months; surveillance for rest pain or tissue loss.

Internal medicine clinic. 62-year-old female with essential hypertension on lisinopril presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort for two days. Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites consistent with urinary tract infection; no fever or flank pain. BP today 148/88 despite medication adherence; amlodipine is added for better control. Plan: nitrofurantoin for five days for the UTI, increased antihypertensive regimen with home BP log, repeat urinalysis if symptoms persist, and follow-up in two weeks to review blood pressure readings and confirm infection resolution.

Inpatient ward note. 37-year-old female admitted with a painful, spreading erythematous, warm area on the left lower leg with tender red streaking up the calf, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis; started on IV cefazolin. She has type 1 diabetes mellitus on an insulin pump and a history of alcohol use disorder with relapse last month; alcohol withdrawal monitored, thiamine continued. Exam also reveals elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, and lower extremity edema; BNP markedly elevated; echo with reduced ejection fraction — decompensated heart failure; diuresed with IV furosemide with good response. Plan: continue antibiotics, diuresis, insulin management, addiction consult, discharge planning with cardiology follow-up.

Inpatient medicine admission. 80-year-old female presenting with sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia; CT angiogram demonstrates pulmonary embolism involving the left main and segmental pulmonary arteries. Started on heparin drip. Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites with dysuria reported, consistent with urinary tract infection; culture sent, started on ceftriaxone. No other urinary abnormalities on imaging. Hospital course: oxygen weaning to nasal cannula, transition to apixaban anticipated. Monitoring INR not required with DOAC; renal function adequate for oral anticoagulation. Urology not consulted given uncomplicated infection. Plan: complete antibiotic course, anticoagulation education, Doppler of lower extremities, discharge when ambulating and stable on room air or baseline oxygen.

CC: facial pressure x 5 days. 54F presents to urgent care with pressure over maxillary region, purulent nasal discharge, low-grade fever, and reduced smell. Worse when bending forward. No cough, no dental pain. Exam: T 100.4, tenderness to percussion over both maxillary sinuses, nasal mucosa edematous with yellow-green drainage, postnasal drip visible. TM's clear. Likely acute bacterial sinusitis given duration, purulence and facial tenderness. Started amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 BID x 10 days, saline rinses, fluticasone nasal spray. Return if worsening headache, vision changes or fever > 102.

Hospital admission, telemetry ward. 72-year-old female with asthma presenting with wheezing and dyspnea for three days, treated with nebulized albuterol and ipratropium, prednisone 40 mg daily started; peak flows improving. She also describes months of constant worry, muscle tension, sleeplessness, plus discrete episodes of palpitations, trembling, and fear of dying lasting twenty minutes — consistent with generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks; sertraline to be initiated at 25 mg daily after medical issues stabilize. On admission creatinine was 2.6 from baseline 0.9 with reduced urine output, acute kidney injury, likely prerenal plus NSAID effect; nephrology consulted, IV fluids given, creatinine now 1.6. Continue asthma therapy, monitor renal function daily, psychiatric consultation for anxiety management.

Telehealth visit. 67-year-old female with long-standing irritable bowel syndrome reports recurrent abdominal cramping relieved by bowel movements, alternating constipation and diarrhea, and bloating worsened by stress; no alarm features, weight stable, recent colonoscopy normal. Symptoms consistent with IBS, managed with dietary modification, peppermint oil, and a low-FODMAP trial. Routine labs revealed 25-OH vitamin D of 14 ng/mL, consistent with vitamin D deficiency; she reports minimal sun exposure. Plan: cholecalciferol 2000 units daily with recheck in 3 months, continue IBS management with symptom diary, fiber adjustment, reassurance given benign workup, follow-up in 3 months.

Telehealth follow-up. 75-year-old female with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and adalimumab reports persistent bilateral knee pain and new thoracic/low back discomfort over the past month. Knee pain is worse with standing and climbing stairs, consistent with degenerative osteoarthritis superimposed on her inflammatory disease. Back pain is mechanical in quality without radiculopathy. Exam (limited video): mild swelling of MCP joints, bilateral knee crepitus with varus deformity, no erythema. Plan: continue DMARD therapy, add acetaminophen, order knee x-rays, PT referral for dorsalgia, and rheumatology follow-up in 3 months.

Hospital admission. 33-year-old female admitted with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. CT pulmonary angiogram shows a segmental pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe — started on apixaban. She reports heavy daily alcohol use, roughly a bottle of vodka daily for several years, with morning shakes — alcohol use disorder; withdrawal risk monitored with CIWA scoring, thiamine given, counseling and detox referral arranged. She also reports diffuse muscle aches and bilateral leg pain attributed to myalgia, likely multifactorial; symptomatic treatment with heat and acetaminophen. Plan: continue anticoagulation, repeat imaging outpatient, addiction medicine follow-up, abstinence support.

60-year-old female admitted after presenting with tremor and elevated blood pressure following heavy drinking; reports daily alcohol use of a pint of spirits for the past decade with morning drinking to steady her hands — alcohol use disorder, moderate to severe. She also smokes a pack of cigarettes daily with strong cravings, consistent with nicotine dependence. CIWA score 8, improving with symptom-triggered lorazepam; thiamine and folate given. Plan: complete alcohol withdrawal protocol, initiate naltrexone prior to discharge with addiction medicine follow-up and relapse-prevention counseling; start nicotine replacement patch with behavioral support, encourage abstinence from both substances, and arrange primary care follow-up within one week.

ED visit. 69-year-old male presents with two days of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, crampy lower abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever after a picnic. Stool studies positive for Campylobacter; fecal leukocytes present, consistent with infectious gastroenteritis and colitis. Exam: diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritonitis. Also reports dysuria and urinary frequency; urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrites, consistent with a urinary tract infection. Additionally, he endorses two weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and appetite loss meeting criteria for a single major depressive episode; PHQ-9 score 16. Plan: supportive hydration, azithromycin for the colitis, nitrofurantoin for the UTI, and initiated sertraline with psychiatry referral and safety planning.

Urology clinic. 85-year-old man evaluated for progressive urinary frequency, nocturia four times nightly, hesitancy, weak stream, and sensation of incomplete emptying over the past year. No hematuria or incontinence. Exam: benign, symmetrically enlarged prostate on digital rectal exam, smooth, no nodules. Post-void residual 110 mL. PSA 2.1, stable. Findings consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Started on tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly; discussed option of finasteride if symptoms persist. Cystoscopy not indicated at this time. Plan: symptom diary, repeat post-void residual in 6 weeks, uroflowmetry if inadequate response, counsel on alarm symptoms including retention and infection; follow-up visit in 2 months.

Inpatient admission, 18-year-old female brought in after several days of heavy binge drinking with poor oral intake. History consistent with alcohol use disorder with repeated withdrawal episodes. Complains of heartburn and retrosternal burning, chronic, worse lying flat; endoscopically confirmed GERD previously, on pantoprazole. Labs show acute kidney injury: creatinine 2.4 mg/dL from baseline 0.7, BUN 38, consistent with prerenal injury from dehydration. Receiving IV fluids, pantoprazole continued, thiamine given. Nephrology consulted; renal function improving. Alcohol counseling initiated and detox referral placed.

ED-to-admission note. 38-year-old man with 2 days of severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and vomiting after a family barbecue; stool studies sent, presumed infectious gastroenteritis and colitis. He also reports recurrent left lower quadrant pain with intermittent fever over recent months; CT abdomen today shows sigmoid diverticular disease with mild pericolonic stranding but no abscess or perforation. Labs notable for creatinine 2.8 (baseline unknown), BUN 48, oliguria — acute kidney failure, likely prerenal from volume depletion. Plan: admit to medical ward for IV rehydration, antiemetics, bowel rest with gradual advance, monitor renal function and urine output every 8 hours, stool culture and C. difficile testing, clear liquid diet then high-fiber education once recovered, GI follow-up for diverticular disease, recheck creatinine prior to discharge.

ED note, 43F presenting with 2 days of left calf swelling, warmth, and pain worse with ambulation. Exam: left calf 3 cm larger than right, tenderness along deep venous system, mild pitting edema, Homans positive. D-dimer elevated; lower extremity duplex ultrasound demonstrates non-compressible left popliteal vein with echogenic thrombus — acute deep vein thrombosis. No PE symptoms; chest clear, sats 98%. Started on apixaban 10 mg BID, LMWH bridge not needed. Hematology consulted. Discharge with anticoagulation, compression stockings, return precautions for dyspnea or chest pain.

Primary care follow-up. 68-year-old male with type 1 diabetes mellitus on basal-bolus insulin (glargine 22 u nightly, lispro 6-8 u with meals) presents for management. Also has hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 20 mg and chronic kidney disease — latest eGFR 38, creatinine 1.9, urine albumin/creatinine ratio elevated; continues lisinopril. Reports recurrent abdominal and pelvic pain over the past month, intermittent and crampy; exam shows soft, mildly tender lower abdomen without masses; urinalysis negative, awaiting outpatient CT. A1c 7.4%. Exam: no pedal edema, sensation intact. Plan: continue insulin regimen, hold metformin given renal function, statin continued, nephrology follow-up, schedule abdominal CT for pain evaluation, recheck renal panel in 3 months.

Telehealth mental health session, 51-year-old woman with several months of intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance of driving following a serious motor vehicle collision last year. She startles easily, sleeps poorly, and reports flashbacks of the crash. PHQ-9 and PTSD checklist consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder following severe stressor exposure; no psychosis or mania. Exam limited via video; affect constricted, appropriate. Plan: continue trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy weekly, begin sertraline 25 mg titrating to 100 mg, prazosin for nightmares, safety planning, and follow-up in two weeks.

62M admitted to the hospital ward with 4 days of fever, productive cough with rust-colored sputum, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. CXR: right lower lobe infiltrate. Pneumonia, unspecified organism, treated empirically with ceftriaxone and azithromycin after cultures sent. During admission he reports chronic heartburn and regurgitation, worse when supine, consistent with gastro-esophageal reflux disease; also epigastric tenderness without melena, felt to represent gastritis/duodenitis — started on pantoprazole and scheduled for EGD once stable. Exam: crackles right base, mild epigastric tenderness, no peritoneal signs. Plan: complete antibiotic course, continue PPI, EGD before discharge or shortly after, dietary counseling, follow-up chest imaging in 6 weeks.

ED evaluation. 37-year-old male presents with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain of 12 hours, anorexia, nausea, and low-grade fever. Exam: RLQ tenderness with guarding and positive Rovsing sign; WBC 15.2 with left shift; CT abdomen shows a dilated, inflamed appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding consistent with acute appendicitis. Of note, he was admitted last month for an ischemic stroke, presenting with left arm weakness; MRI then showed a right MCA territory infarct, and he remains on aspirin and atorvastatin with residual mild left hand clumsiness. Plan: general surgery consulted for appendectomy tonight; continue stroke medications perioperatively; neurology to follow.

65-year-old male seen on the geriatric ward. His wife reports progressive memory decline over two years with disorientation, word-finding difficulty, and impaired daily functioning; cognitive testing shows significant deficits consistent with Alzheimer disease, and donepezil was started. He is a veteran with combat-related PTSD, experiencing nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance of crowds, managed with sertraline and trauma-focused therapy referrals. Labs also confirm chronic kidney disease with eGFR 45, stable, monitored by nephrology. Plan: continue donepezil with reassessment of cognition, continue sertraline with PTSD therapy follow-up, maintain renal monitoring and NSAID avoidance, and arrange caregiver support services for the family.

40-year-old male, telehealth visit for medication refills. Epilepsy with recurrent focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, last episode three weeks ago; on levo-carbamazepine 400 mg BID, levels therapeutic, no aura change. He smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and is nicotine dependent; expressed readiness to quit, agreed to start varenicline taper and nicotine replacement. Also reports intermittent diffuse abdominal and pelvic pain over the past month, non-bloody bowel movements, no fever; exam limited by telehealth, advised ER if pain localizes or worsens; will arrange in-person abdominal exam and consider imaging if symptoms persist. Plan: continue antiseizure medication, driving restrictions reviewed, smoking cessation counseling documented, follow-up in four weeks or sooner for pain.

ED note. 49-year-old female presents with acute pleuritic right-sided chest pain and dyspnea. CT angiogram of chest demonstrates a filling defect in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery consistent with pulmonary embolism. Labs notable for creatinine 2.6 mg/dL, up from baseline 1.0, with reduced urine output, consistent with acute kidney injury. Started on therapeutic heparin infusion; nephrology consulted for the renal failure, holding nephrotoxic agents and monitoring urine output. Admitted to stepdown unit for anticoagulation and renal monitoring. Plan: transition to apixaban when appropriate, avoid contrast studies, repeat basic metabolic panel, and evaluate for provoking factors. Stable currently, no hemodynamic compromise.

Inpatient ward note. 20-year-old man admitted with right-sided weakness and slurred speech; MRI shows acute left MCA territory ischemic infarct, thrombolysis window missed. He has known type 2 diabetes mellitus, poorly controlled, on metformin and basal insulin, A1c 11.2%. During admission he develops a spreading erythematous, warm plaque on the right calf with a tender red streak tracking up the medial leg, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. Plan: stroke unit monitoring, physical therapy, aspirin and atorvastatin, continued insulin regimen with endocrinology consult; IV cefazolin for the cellulitis/lymphangitis with daily wound assessment and limb elevation.

ED note, 58-year-old male presents with anorexia, nausea, and 18 hours of right lower quadrant pain. Exam: RLQ tenderness, guarding, positive Rovsing and McBurney signs; CT abdomen shows a dilated appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding — acute appendicitis; surgery consulted, scheduled for laparoscopic appendectomy. He also reports a severe unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia earlier this week, typical of his migraines; sumatriptan PRN continued. Productive cough with scattered rhonchi, no consolidation, consistent with acute bronchitis; given guaifenesin and dextromethorphan, no antibiotics. Well-demarcated scaly plaques on elbows consistent with known psoriasis; continue topical clobetasol.

ED to surgical admission. 58-year-old female presents with 18 hours of right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, nausea; temperature 38.2, tenderness with guarding at McBurney's point, WBC 15.4 — acute appendicitis confirmed on CT; general surgery consulted for laparoscopic appendectomy. Incidentally noted hyperlipidemia: total cholesterol 268, LDL 172 on this admission's labs, not previously diagnosed; to begin atorvastatin postoperatively after repeat fasting panel. Plan: appendectomy tonight, NPO, IV antibiotics, lipid follow-up in primary care after discharge.

Psychology telehealth session. 61-year-old female with BMI 30.2, class I obesity, here for ongoing management of post-traumatic stress disorder following a motor vehicle accident three years ago. Continues to have intrusive flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of driving, and hypervigilance; PCL-5 score 58, consistent with chronic PTSD. She also describes recurrent abdominal pain with bloating and alternating constipation and diarrhea over the past year, relieved with defecation, without alarm features; workup including celiac serology and colonoscopy was normal, consistent with irritable bowel syndrome. Plan: continue sertraline 100 mg daily, resume trauma-focused CPT sessions weekly, begin low-FODMAP diet trial with dietitian referral, and address weight through structured activity plan given stress-related eating. Follow-up in four weeks.

Urgent care clinic. 41-year-old male with two days of watery diarrhea, six to eight stools daily, with cramping abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever after a family barbecue. No blood in stool. Concurrent sore throat, rhinorrhea, and dry cough that began the same day. Exam: temp 38.1 C, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound, hyperactive bowel sounds, pharynx erythematous without exudate, scattered wheezes with coarse rhonchi on chest auscultation. Stool culture sent; likely infectious gastroenteritis and colitis plus acute upper respiratory infection and acute bronchitis. Supportive care with oral rehydration, ondansetron as needed, guaifenesin, and rest. Return if unable to keep fluids down or if bloody stool develops.

Outpatient clinic, SOAP. 88-year-old female here for follow-up of chronic heartburn, retrosternal burning after meals and when lying flat, occasional sour regurgitation at night, symptoms several times weekly for months. Exam: comfortable, abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Symptoms classic for GERD; no dysphagia, weight loss, or bleeding reported. Plan: lifestyle measures (elevate head of bed, avoid late meals, smaller portions); start pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 8 weeks; trial taper afterward; return sooner if dysphagia, vomiting, or weight loss develops. Follow-up in 8 weeks to assess response and consider step-down therapy.

34-year-old male admitted to the ward with acute kidney failure, oliguria, and rising creatinine after starting NSAIDs for a gout flare of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint exam shows a swollen, warm, tender great toe consistent with acute gouty arthritis; uric acid elevated. He also has untreated hyperlipidemia with markedly elevated LDL on this admission's panel. He reports longstanding urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia; exam confirms an enlarged, smooth prostate consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Plan: hold NSAIDs, IV fluids, monitor creatinine and urine output, colchicine for gout once renal function stabilizes, start atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia, and continue tamsulosin for BPH symptoms.

ED visit. 87-year-old female presents with intermittent right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, radiating to right shoulder, lasting 1-2 hours, associated with nausea. Afebrile, no jaundice. Exam: tender RUQ, positive Murphy's sign. Labs: WBC 9.2, normal bilirubin and LFTs. RUQ ultrasound: multiple gallstones in the gallbladder, no wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, common duct normal caliber. Impression: symptomatic cholelithiasis, biliary colic without cholecystitis. Plan: low-fat diet, analgesia, surgical consultation for elective cholecystectomy, return for fever or persistent pain.

Hospital admission. 21-year-old female admitted with pleuritic right chest pain, fever, and hypoxia; chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate consistent with pneumonia, started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Doppler ultrasound of the right leg reveals an acute deep vein thrombosis of the popliteal vein; started on heparin drip. She reports chronic mid-back pain and muscle tension for which she uses a heating pad and naproxen. She also describes months of excessive worry, restlessness, poor sleep, and recent panic attacks with palpitations — consistent with generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks; psychology consulted. Plan: transition to apixaban, continue antibiotics, NSAIDs for dorsalgia, start sertraline, anxiety management referral.

Internal medicine clinic: 33-year-old male here for follow-up. Fasting lipid panel shows total cholesterol 288, LDL 210, triglycerides 320 — mixed hyperlipidemia; started on atorvastatin. Long-standing epilepsy, well controlled on levetiracetam 500 mg BID; no seizures in 14 months, no aura today. Also reports calf claudication with walking, diminished dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally — chronic peripheral vascular disease; ankle-brachial index 0.7 on right. Plan: continue antiepileptic, statin therapy, ABI surveillance, vascular surgery referral, daily aspirin.

Emergency Department. 76-year-old male brought in with fever, productive cough, and dyspnea. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate; treated empirically for pneumonia with ceftriaxone and azithromycin pending cultures, organism not yet identified. On telemetry he is found to be in an irregularly irregular rhythm without discernible P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation with flutter; rate 112, hemodynamically stable. Rate control started with metoprolol; anticoagulation decision deferred pending admission. Plan: admit to telemetry ward, continue antibiotics, serial troponins, echo, and anticoagulation discussion.

Urgent care note, 27-year-old male with 2 days of intermittent diffuse abdominal and pelvic pain, crampy in nature, associated with nausea but no vomiting, no fever. No diarrhea, no dysuria. Exam: abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness, more pronounced in the lower abdomen and pelvic region, no rebound or guarding, no CVA tenderness, no hernia. Bowel sounds normal. Appendicitis and testicular pathology clinically unlikely; urinalysis unremarkable, CBC normal. Given nonspecific abdominal and pelvic pain, likely nonsurgical etiology. Plan: symptomatic management with antispasmodic and heat, clear liquids advancing as tolerated, return precautions for worsening pain, fever, or vomiting; follow-up in 48 hours if not improving; no imaging indicated at this time.

38F hematology clinic visit. On levothyroxine 100 mcg daily for hypothyroidism; TSH today 7.8, free T4 low-normal — dose under-suppressed, increased to 125 mcg daily, recheck TSH in 6 weeks. Also followed for ADHD on lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily, symptoms well controlled, no side effects, PHQ-9 negative. Presents today with two-day history of right thigh swelling and pain; ultrasound reveals acute deep vein thrombosis in the right femoral vein. Initiated rivaroxaban 15 mg BID x21 days then 20 mg daily, advised to avoid prolonged immobility, given return precautions for pulmonary embolism symptoms. Will arrange D-dimer/ultrasound surveillance per protocol. Return in 3 weeks for anticoagulation reassessment and thyroid labs.

Urgent care note. 60-year-old man with 2 days of sore throat, odynophagia, and low-grade fever; no cough. Exam: pharynx erythematous with tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical adenopathy; rapid strep positive. Diagnosis: acute streptococcal pharyngitis; started penicillin VK for 10 days. Also long-standing gastro-esophageal reflux disease with heartburn and regurgitation, especially after meals and when supine; on omeprazole 20 mg daily with partial response. Advised to take antibiotic with food, avoid late meals, elevate head of bed, avoid NSAIDs. Plan: continue PPI, reassess reflux symptoms in 6 weeks with consideration of step-up therapy; return if throat symptoms persist beyond the antibiotic course.

72-year-old female attending rheumatology clinic. She has long-standing combined inattentive and hyperactive symptoms dating to childhood, previously diagnosed ADHD, managed with methylphenidate ER which she tolerates well; continue current dose. She presents today with bilateral knee pain worse with activity and stairs, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Exam: crepitus in both knees, varus alignment, joint line tenderness, no effusion or warmth. X-rays: medial compartment joint space narrowing and osteophytes, findings of osteoarthritis of both knees. Plan: acetaminophen, quadriceps strengthening, weight-bearing activity as tolerated, consider intra-articular steroid injection if refractory.

Endocrinology clinic. 66-year-old male with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 20, on insulin pump, A1c 7.8%, no active retinopathy. Also with well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques over elbows and knees consistent with psoriasis; topical corticosteroid and vitamin D analog prescribed, dermatology follow-up. Reports two-month history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and loss of interest; PHQ-9 score 16 consistent with a single major depressive episode; started on sertraline, counseled on safety, psychology referral. Epilepsy with recurrent seizures, most recent generalized tonic-clonic eight months ago; continues levetiracetam, levels therapeutic, driving restrictions reviewed. Insulin regimen fine-tuned, continuous glucose monitor data reviewed. Return visit in six weeks.

GI clinic. 42-year-old male with intermittent left lower quadrant cramping and a history of diverticulosis on prior colonoscopy — diverticular disease of the intestine, currently without acute inflammation. He reports a low-fiber diet. Liver ultrasound ordered for mild transamidase elevation showed diffuse hyperechogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis (fatty liver disease). Plan: high-fiber diet, fiber supplement, avoid NSAIDs, weight and alcohol counseling, repeat LFTs in 3 months, surveillance colonoscopy per schedule.

Inpatient consult note. 68-year-old male admitted with a painful, spreading erythematous area with red streaking on the right lower leg, warm and tender, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis; started on IV cefazolin. PMH: type 1 diabetes mellitus on basal-bolus insulin, COPD on tiotropium and rescue albuterol with a 30 pack-year history, and adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder maintained on methylphenidate. Glucose trending 180-220, insulin regimen continued; lungs with mild expiratory wheeze but no exacerbation. Plan: complete 5-day antibiotic course, mark erythema borders, transition to oral antibiotics, pulmonary to optimize COPD therapy, continue ADHD stimulant with monitoring.

89-year-old female seen on the geriatric ward. She presents with acute onset of a painful, red, swollen first right metatarsophalangeal joint; arthrocentesis shows negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals, confirming gout. Started on colchicine with improvement. She also reports urinary frequency, urgency and dysuria for two days; urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrites, and culture grows E. coli, consistent with a urinary tract infection. Exam: no suprapubic tenderness, afebrile; no flank pain. Plan: colchicine taper, allopurinol deferred until flare resolves, nitrofurantoin 5 days, increased fluids, repeat culture after therapy, monitor renal function.

Clinic visit. 52-year-old male accompanied by his wife, who reports progressive memory decline over the past two years — difficulty recalling recent conversations, misplacing items, getting lost driving familiar routes. Cognitive testing shows impaired delayed recall and disorientation to date; diagnosis of Alzheimer disease discussed, started on donepezil 10 mg nightly. He also reports diffuse muscle aches and bilateral leg pain for several weeks, worse after activity, without joint swelling or weakness; attributed to soft tissue myalgia, managed with heat, stretching, and acetaminophen as needed. Exam: benign joint exam, no point tenderness over joints, mild muscle tenderness bilaterally. Plan: repeat cognitive testing in 3 months, MRI brain to exclude other causes, caregiver support referral, and follow-up for limb pain if not improving.

Pulmonary clinic. 73-year-old woman, transgender with retained prostate, presents for COPD management — chronic productive cough and exertional dyspnea; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.52 with minimal reversibility, on tiotropium and alendronate-sparing regimen of dual bronchodilators, with prednisone bursts twice yearly. She describes decades-old abdominal pain relieved by defecation, alternating bowel habit, and bloating without alarm features — irritable bowel syndrome, managed with dietary modification and antispasmodics. Recent right upper quadrant ultrasound also incidentally revealed multiple gallstones in a well-filled gallbladder without wall thickening or duct dilation — asymptomatic cholelithiasis; surgery discussed, she declines for now. She also reports urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia; post-void residual 120 mL, prostate enlarged and smooth on exam — benign prostatic hyperplasia; started on tamsulosin. Plan: continue inhalers, pulmonary rehab, fiber diet, uroflow follow-up, GI review.

Telehealth follow-up. 55-year-old female seen after recent ischemic stroke involving the left MCA territory; residual mild right-hand weakness, on atorvastatin and aspirin, physical therapy progressing. Long-standing essential hypertension, maintained on lisinopril 20 mg daily; home readings averaging 132/84. Also carries a diagnosis of combined-type ADHD, managed with extended-release methylphenidate; reports improved focus and task completion at work. No seizure activity, no recurrent focal deficits. Plan: continue stroke secondary prevention, recheck lipids, BP log review in 4 weeks, renew stimulant prescription with pharmacy as scheduled.

Telehealth visit, 77-year-old female with known chronic kidney disease, stage 3b (eGFR 38). Reports 3 days of sore throat with painful swallowing, odynophagia, no cough; also urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic burning for 2 days. Rapid strep positive, consistent with acute pharyngitis. Urinalysis from outside lab shows pyuria and nitrites, consistent with a lower urinary tract infection. Exam limited by video; no visible tonsillar exudate reported but anterior cervical adenopathy per patient self-palpation. Plan: penicillin VK 500 mg BID x10 days for pharyngitis; nitrofurantoin 5 days for the UTI, chosen for renal tolerance given her CKD; increase fluids; repeat urinalysis after treatment and BMP in 2 weeks to monitor kidney function.

Neurology clinic. 65-year-old male with 20-year history of recurrent severe unilateral pulsatile headaches, lasting 4-12 hours, with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, and occasional visual aura. Attacks have increased to 4 per month, interfering with work. Neurologic exam normal; no red flags. Impression: migraine with aura, frequency now warranting prophylaxis. Started topiramate 25 mg nightly with titration; continued rizatriptan 10 mg for acute attacks, limited to 8 days per month to avoid medication-overuse headache. Headache diary provided. Avoid identified triggers including skipped meals and poor sleep. Follow-up in 8 weeks to assess attack frequency and tolerability.

38F telehealth visit for weight management. BMI 31.4, weight 186 lb, height 5'4". Meets criteria for obesity class I; waist circumference 38 inches. No bariatric surgery history. Screened for secondary causes — thyroid studies normal. Discussed nutrition plan with reduced caloric intake, referral to dietitian, structured exercise program 150 min/week, behavioral counseling. Offered GLP-1 agonist semaglutide; patient interested, baseline A1c and lipids ordered. Reviewed associated risks including metabolic and joint strain. Patient motivated; goal 10% weight loss over 6 months. Follow-up telehealth visit in 6 weeks with weight log. No depression or eating disorder screen positives.

Internal medicine clinic. 67-year-old male for follow-up of elevated blood pressure and reflux. Home readings 150-160 systolic. Denies chest pain. Reports heartburn 3-4 times weekly, worse after meals and when lying flat, relieved by antacids; occasional regurgitation. Exam: BP 152/88, HR 76, lungs clear, no edema. Plan: continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, increase to 40 mg given inadequate control, recheck BP in 4 weeks with basic metabolic panel. For GERD: start omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast, lifestyle counseling to avoid late meals and elevate head of bed, reassess symptoms in 6-8 weeks.

23-year-old male seen in the ED for left calf pain and swelling for two days. Ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible left popliteal vein thrombus; DVT confirmed, started on apixaban. He reports a recent panic attack with chest pounding drove him to seek care; he describes ongoing pervasive worry, restlessness, and recurrent panic episodes with dizziness and fear of losing control, consistent with generalized anxiety and panic disorder. He also has a history of two gout flares in the right great toe, last one three months ago, managed with colchicine. Plan: anticoagulation, outpatient hematology follow-up, behavioral health referral for anxiety, allopurinol discussion with PCP, discharge home.

53M evaluated in vascular clinic for bilateral calf cramping and aching, worse with ambulation, plus persistent coolness and bluish discoloration of both feet. Pulses are diminished at the dorsalis pedis; ABI 0.7 on the right, 0.75 on the left. Findings are consistent with other peripheral vascular disease beyond simple claudication — small vessel involvement with acrocyanosis-like changes; no ulceration or gangrene. No history of procedures. Plan: initiate supervised exercise program, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, statin for vascular protection, foot care education, duplex ultrasound surveillance in 3 months, return sooner if rest pain or tissue breakdown develops.

Hospital ward progress note. 72-year-old female admitted with decompensated heart failure (volume overload, orthopnea, JVD, bilateral crackles, 2+ lower extremity edema); on furosemide with improving daily weights. Past history includes Alzheimer disease with moderate cognitive impairment (donepezil, caregiver assistance with ADLs) and epilepsy on levetiracetam, seizure-free for 2 years. She also reports chronic bilateral knee pain with crepitus and varus deformity consistent with osteoarthritis, limiting ambulation. Exam: lungs clearing, knees with bony enlargement, reduced flexion, no effusion. Plan: continue diuresis and daily weights for CHF; maintain donepezil and levetiracetam; acetaminophen scheduled and PT for knee osteoarthritis, defer joint replacement discussion given cognitive status; case management for discharge planning.

Telehealth follow-up, psychiatry. 69-year-old woman with longstanding inattention, distractibility, and difficulty completing tasks, consistent with ADHD, well controlled on lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily. She reports no tics, appetite loss, or insomnia. Additionally, she has episodic unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea, consistent with migraines, occurring about twice monthly; sumatriptan aborts most attacks. Plan: continue stimulant therapy, monitor blood pressure and pulse, continue PRN triptan, headache diary, follow-up in three months.

Movement disorders clinic. 24-year-old woman with young-onset Parkinson disease, diagnosed 2 years ago, on carbidopa-levodopa and pramipexole, presents for follow-up of tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity, currently well controlled. She also reports a chronic itchy rash over her hands and wrists with periodic flares; exam shows dry, scaly, excoriated eczematous patches on the dorsal hands and wrists, consistent with eczematous dermatitis; no infection noted. Assessment: stable Parkinson disease; atopic dermatitis flare. Plan: continue current antiparkinsonian regimen with no dose changes, physical therapy referral; for the dermatitis, advise fragrance-free emollients twice daily, apply triamcinolone 0.1% ointment BID x2 weeks, and avoid known irritants; follow-up in 3 months.

Inpatient ward note. 28-year-old female admitted with acute appendicitis confirmed on CT, underwent laparoscopic appendectomy on hospital day 1; recovering well. She has a history of epigastric burning pain diagnosed as gastritis and duodenitis on endoscopy last year, maintained on omeprazole 20 mg daily. She also carries a longstanding diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome with recurrent cramping and alternating bowel habits, managed with dietary modification. Postoperatively she became oliguric with creatinine rising from 0.7 to 2.6, consistent with acute kidney injury/failure; BUN 42. Plan: IV fluids, hold NSAIDs, monitor renal function daily, continue PPI, GI follow-up.

Primary care clinic, 53-year-old woman presenting for left lower quadrant abdominal discomfort and changes in bowel habit over the past month. CT abdomen performed earlier shows sigmoid diverticula without abscess or perforation; findings consistent with diverticular disease of the intestine. Exam: mild LLQ tenderness, no peritoneal signs. She also reports smoking one pack per day for thirty years and expresses interest in quitting. Plan: high-fiber diet, psyllium supplement, avoid seeds/nuts per preference, start varenicline taper and nicotine replacement patch for nicotine dependence, arrange smoking cessation counseling, and follow up in six weeks.

Vascular clinic note. 33-year-old man referred for exertional right calf pain and coolness of the right foot for several months, worse with walking, relieved by rest — symptoms consistent with peripheral vascular disease. No diabetes, nonsmoker. Exam: right foot slightly cooler and paler than left, weakly palpable dorsalis pedis pulse, capillary refill 3 seconds. Ankle-brachial index 0.85 on the right, 1.1 on the left. Duplex ultrasound shows diminished flow in the right lower extremity without critical ischemia. Plan: supervised exercise program, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 81 mg daily, lipid panel ordered, reassess ABI in 3 months, return sooner if rest pain or tissue changes develop.

Hospital admission. 21-year-old female transferred from outside ED. Presented with fever, rigors, hypotension, and lactic acidosis of 4.2 meeting criteria for sepsis — source under investigation, cultures pending, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation initiated. Concurrently found to have ST-elevation in the inferior leads; emergent catheterization showed thrombotic occlusion of the right coronary artery treated with thrombectomy and stenting — acute myocardial infarction. History of gout, currently with a swollen, erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint; colchicine started, allopurinol held during acute flare. Also carries chronic kidney disease, baseline creatinine 1.9, now 2.3; nephrology consulted, all medications renally dosed. Plan: continue antibiotics, dual antiplatelet therapy, cardiology and nephrology follow-up, serum uric acid monitoring after flare resolves.

Urology clinic. 62-year-old male presents with 4 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and foul-smelling urine without fever or flank pain, consistent with a lower urinary tract infection; urinalysis shows pyuria, nitrites, and leukocyte esterase. No prior instrumentation. Exam: abdomen soft, no suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness. Started on nitrofurantoin for 5 days with increased fluid intake. Plan: repeat urinalysis if symptoms persist, culture sent, follow-up as needed, discussed preventive measures including adequate hydration.

ED visit. 73-year-old male presents with four days of facial pressure over the right maxillary area, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and low-grade fever. No cough, no dental pain. Exam: temperature 37.9 C, tenderness to palpation over right maxillary and frontal sinuses, purulent drainage from right middle turbinate, opaque right maxillary sinus on transillumination. Clinical picture consistent with acute bacterial sinusitis. Started amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 twice daily for 10 days, intranasal saline rinses, and fluticasone spray. Return precautions for worsening headache, vision changes, or periorbital swelling. Discharged home in stable condition.

Telehealth mental health follow-up. 42-year-old male veteran seen by video for ongoing nightmares, hypervigilance, and flashbacks following a motor vehicle accident eight months ago. He avoids driving and reports intrusive memories, poor sleep, and exaggerated startle. Consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder; adjustment difficulties persist after job loss. Sertraline increased to 100 mg daily, prazosin at bedtime for nightmares. Also reports bilateral knee pain with crepitus on stairs, worse this month; exam limited via video, but prior imaging showed tricompartmental osteoarthritis of the right knee. Continue NSAIDs as needed, refer to physiotherapy, consider intra-articular steroid injection at next in-person visit. PTSD-focused CBT scheduled biweekly.

Nephrology clinic, 21-year-old man with chronic kidney disease, stage 3, likely reflux nephropathy, eGFR 44 with baseline creatinine 1.9; managed with sodium bicarbonate and tight BP control. He reports drinking six to eight beers daily for the past three years with unsuccessful quit attempts and morning cravings, and also smokes a half pack of cigarettes daily. Exam: pallor, trace pedal edema, otherwise unremarkable. Plan: continue CKD management, avoid nephrotoxins, nephrology dietitian referral, initiate alcohol use disorder treatment with naltrexone and referral to addiction counseling, nicotine replacement therapy for tobacco dependence, and repeat renal panel in one month.

78M outpatient neurology/psychiatry co-visit. Longstanding epilepsy, well controlled on levetiracetam 500 mg BID, no seizures in 14 months, level therapeutic. Reports escalating worry over the past 6 months, difficulty controlling worry, poor sleep, muscle tension — consistent with generalized anxiety disorder. Also describes discrete episodes of sudden intense fear with palpitations and fear of dying lasting 10-15 minutes, panic attacks occurring twice monthly, avoided leaving home alone — panic disorder features. Started sertraline 25 mg daily titrating to 50 mg, cautious for seizure threshold; referred for CBT. EEG unchanged from baseline. Continue levetiracetam, no driving restrictions changes. Follow-up in 6 weeks with GAD-7 and seizure diary.

Ward note. 84-year-old female admitted with abdominal and pelvic pain, CT showing multiple sigmoid diverticula without abscess or perforation — diverticular disease of intestine, treated with clear liquids and antibiotics. Her history includes thyrotoxicosis managed with methimazole 5 mg daily (TSH suppressed at last check) and Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily. Exam: mild LLQ tenderness without rebound, fine resting tremor and bradykinesia, no thyroid enlargement. Pain is controlled with acetaminophen. Plan: continue methimazole, maintain Parkinson medication schedule on time to avoid worsening motor symptoms, advance diet as tolerated, repeat TSH and free T4, PT for mobility, discharge planning once pain resolves.

88-year-old male seen in clinic for routine follow-up. Fasting lipid panel: total cholesterol 232, LDL 148, HDG 42, triglycerides 176. No prior statin therapy. Patient active and living independently; exam benign, no xanthomas. Discussed diagnosis of hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular risk in context of age. Given competing considerations at 88, elected moderate-intensity therapy: atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Will repeat lipid panel and hepatic panel in 3 months. Advised Mediterranean-style diet and continued activity. Tolerating well so far, no myalgias reported at telephone check-in.

54M pulmonary clinic follow-up. Ten-year history of COPD, now with chronic productive cough and exertional dyspnea; spirometry FEV1/FVC 0.52, FEV1 48% predicted, minimal bronchodilator response. CAT score 18. Exam: diminished breath sounds bilaterally, prolonged expiration, no wheeze today. Current regimen: tiotropium daily, albuterol PRN with good technique. Added dual therapy with indacaterol/glycopyrrolate, pulmonary rehab referral, and annual influenza plus pneumococcal vaccination confirmed. Discussed exacerbation action plan and oral steroid/antibiotic pack for severe episodes. Oxygen saturation 93% on room air, no resting desaturation on 6-minute walk. Follow-up spirometry and CAT score in 3 months.

Endocrinology clinic: 63-year-old female with longstanding diabetes mellitus. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 19, on basal-bolus insulin (glargine and lispro), but over recent years has developed progressive insulin resistance requiring very high doses, and A1c of 8.9% with features of type 2 diabetes superimposed on her underlying autoimmune disease; metformin added to regimen. Today also evaluated for fatigue; CBC shows hemoglobin 9.8, microcytic indices, ferritin low at 6 — iron deficiency anemia, likely from GI losses; colonoscopy scheduled; started on oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg TID. Plan: continue insulin plus metformin, nutrition review, repeat A1c and CBC in 3 months.

Family medicine clinic: 32-year-old female with facial pain, nasal congestion, and postnasal drip for ten days — acute sinusitis; prescribed amoxicillin and saline rinses. BMI 31 with central adiposity on exam; discussed overweight/obesity, nutrition referral and structured exercise program arranged, baseline fasting glucose and lipids ordered. No headache red flags, afebrile today. Plan: reassess sinus symptoms in 10 days, weight management follow-up in 3 months with dietitian, repeat BMI measurement.

Pulmonary clinic. 80-year-old male with chronic productive cough and exertional dyspnea; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.55 with minimal reversibility, consistent with COPD. On tiotropium daily with albuterol rescue; inhaler technique reviewed, no exacerbations in past 6 months. Labs reveal 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 14 ng/mL, consistent with vitamin D deficiency; started on cholecalciferol 2000 units daily with repeat level in 3 months. Plan: continue pulmonary regimen, annual spirometry, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, follow up in 3 months.

Urgent care visit. 44-year-old male presents with two days of sore throat, painful swallowing, and low-grade fever. No cough. Exam: temperature 38.1°C, pharynx erythematous with tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, Centor score 4, rapid strep positive. Chest clear, no rash. Diagnosis: acute streptococcal pharyngitis. Started on penicillin VK 500 mg twice daily for 10 days with ibuprofen for pain. Advised hydration, rest, and return if unable to swallow fluids or if symptoms worsen after 48 hours. Work note provided.

Orthopedic clinic: 69-year-old female seen for back discomfort and fracture risk assessment. DEXA scan: lumbar spine T-score -3.1, femoral neck -2.7, confirming osteoporosis without evidence of acute or pathological fracture on imaging. 25-OH vitamin D level 14 ng/mL, marked deficiency. No prior fragility fractures. Started cholecalciferol 50,000 units weekly for 8 weeks then maintenance, calcium supplementation, and alendronate 70 mg weekly. Counselled on fall prevention, weight-bearing exercise. Repeat vitamin D level and DEXA in one year; return sooner if any new fracture symptoms.

Primary care clinic. 59-year-old female with sore throat, nasal congestion, cough, and low-grade fever for four days — acute upper respiratory infection, likely viral; supportive care advised, no antibiotics indicated. She has chronic kidney disease, stage 3, with baseline creatinine 1.6 and eGFR 45, attributed to long-standing nephropathy; on lisinopril and follows a renal diet. Avoiding NSAIDs and nephrotoxics for her URRI symptoms; recommended saline rinse, acetaminophen if needed, fluids, and rest. Plan: repeat creatinine in 2 weeks, nephrology follow-up already scheduled, return if symptoms worsen or fever persists beyond a week.

Pulmonology clinic. 73-year-old female with a chronic productive cough and progressive exertional dyspnea; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC of 0.58 with 12% bronchodilator response, consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She is on tiotropium and albuterol as needed. This week she developed sore throat, rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion without fever, consistent with an acute upper respiratory infection; chest exam clear of consolidation. Labs also reveal 25-OH vitamin D of 15 ng/mL, confirming vitamin D deficiency. Plan: continue COPD inhalers, add pulmonary rehabilitation referral, symptomatic care for the upper respiratory infection with fluids and rest, and begin cholecalciferol 1,000 units daily with repeat level in three months. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination discussed.

ED to admission note. 26-year-old male presents with sudden onset right-sided weakness and slurred speech 90 minutes prior to arrival, witnessed by his roommate. Last known well at onset. Exam: right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness (3/5), dysarthria, NIHSS 8. CT head shows no hemorrhage; CT angiogram reveals left MCA occlusion consistent with acute ischemic infarction. No arrhythmia on telemetry; echocardiogram pending. Plan: IV thrombolysis administered within window; admit to stroke unit with neuro checks q1h; aspirin and high-intensity statin to start after 24-hour imaging; PT/OT/SLP evaluations; stroke workup including carotid imaging and prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic source.

Hospital ward progress note. 87-year-old female admitted after acute onset right hemiparesis and aphasia; head MRI shows an acute ischemic infarct in the left MCA territory. She is on a stroke protocol with aspirin and atorvastatin, PT/OT consults placed. Overnight she became oliguric with creatinine rising from 1.1 to 3.4 mg/dL, BUN 62; acute renal failure suspected from dehydration and contrast exposure, with nephrology consulted and fluids adjusted. She also carries a history of obstructive sleep apnea with loud snoring and witnessed apneas, using CPAP at home; CPAP continued during sleep while monitored. Plan: continue stroke care, monitor renal function closely, strict I/O, CPAP at night, and early mobilization.

Pulmonary clinic. 45-year-old female with chronic productive cough and exertional dyspnea; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.62 with minimal bronchodilator response, consistent with COPD. Long history of inhalational exposures. Currently on ipratropium/albuterol nebulizers and started on utibron; exacerbations twice last year. Exam: diminished breath sounds, prolonged expiration, no wheeze today. Plan: pulmonary rehab referral, annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, action plan for exacerbations, follow-up spirometry in 6 months.

ED note. 24-year-old male presents with 2 days of left calf swelling and pain. Doppler ultrasound: acute occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein — deep vein thrombosis. Started on apixaban. He also reports several months of fatigue; hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL with MCV 72 and ferritin 8 ng/mL, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; colonoscopy scheduled as outpatient. Additionally has chronic pruritic, erythematous patches with lichenification on flexor surfaces of both elbows, consistent with atopic dermatitis; triamcinolone 0.1% cream prescribed. Plan: apixaban 10 mg BID x 7 days then 5 mg BID, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, dermatology follow-up, hematology consultation for anemia workup, DVT follow-up in 1 week.

Neurology clinic: 19-year-old male with progressive cognitive decline over three years — short-term memory loss, disorientation, and behavioral changes; workup excluded other causes, and biopsy-confirmed Alzheimer disease, early-onset familial type. He also has hepatomegaly on exam; ultrasound shows diffuse echogenic liver consistent with fatty liver disease, LFTs mildly elevated. Donepezil started, memantine to follow. Liver panel monitoring q3 months, counseling on lifestyle, hepatology referral, and genetic counseling offered for family.

SOAP note, primary care clinic. 49-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 22, on insulin glargine and lispro, last A1c 7.6%. Also carries essential hypertension, treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily, BP today 138/86. Presented with fatigue and pallor for several weeks; labs show hemoglobin 9.8 with low-normal MCV, iron studies unremarkable, no evidence of hemolysis or blood loss on initial workup — anemia, etiology unspecified. Exam: pallor of conjunctivae, no organomegaly. Plan: continue basal-bolus insulin with glucose monitoring; intensify antihypertensive regimen; hematology referral for further anemia evaluation, repeat CBC in 4 weeks; dietitian review.

Neurology clinic follow-up. 57-year-old male with longstanding epilepsy presents after two witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the past month, one with tongue biting and postictal confusion lasting 20 minutes. He admits missed levetiracetam doses over the past several weeks. Exam: alert, no focal deficits; healed tongue laceration. Plan: reinforce adherence, increase levetiracetam to 1000 mg BID, add lamotrigine taper, driving restrictions reiterated, check levetiracetam level and EEG in 4 weeks, seizure diary.

Hospital progress note: 52-year-old male admitted with two days of oliguria and rising creatinine. Serum creatinine 4.1 mg/dL, BUN 62; consistent with acute kidney failure, likely prerenal from recent NSAID overuse for chronic bilateral knee pain. Exam shows crepitus and bony tenderness over both knees, reduced flexion to 90 degrees, classic osteoarthritis. Held nephrotoxins, IV fluids, input/output monitoring. Nephrology consulted. For knee pain, acetaminophen only while renal function recovers; will consider topical therapy and PT once acute kidney injury resolves.

Telehealth visit, 37-year-old female established patient. Reports flashbacks, nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance of crowds since a motor vehicle accident two years ago; symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder, ongoing. Also complains of recurrent pruritic, erythematous patches with scaling on flexor wrists and antecubital fossae, consistent with her chronic eczema flare; topical triamcinolone renewed. Renal function stable with eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2 and chronic changes on ultrasound, consistent with stage 3b chronic kidney disease; continues lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide per nephrology. Plan: continue sertraline and trauma-focused therapy referral, moisturizer regimen, repeat BMP in three months, avoid NSAIDs.

Clinic note. 46-year-old male presents with 3 days of a spreading, warm, erythematous plaque on the left lower leg with a red streaking pattern extending proximally, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. He also reports dysuria and urinary frequency; urinalysis positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase — urinary tract infection. He has known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 100 mcg daily (TSH 6.8 at last check, dose increased to 112 mcg) and a chronic normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, etiology under evaluation. Exam: temperature 100.8 F, tender left leg erythema with lymphangitic streaking, no abscess. Plan: cephalexin 500 mg QID x 7 days, nitrofurantoin for UTI, repeat CBC and TSH in 6 weeks, elevate leg, return if fever persists or erythema spreads.

Hospital admission note. 71-year-old female admitted from the ED with three days of fever, productive cough, dyspnea, and decreased oral intake. Exam: temperature 101.2F, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the left base, dullness to percussion. Chest x-ray reveals a left lower lobe consolidation; white count 15.8 with left shift, procalcitonin elevated. Cultures obtained but no organism identified as yet; treated as pneumonia, unspecified organism, with empiric IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula, incentive spirometry, and IV fluids. Advance care discussion held. Plan: de-escalate antibiotics when cultures finalize, monitor oxygen weaning, and discharge with oral therapy once afebrile and stable.

80-year-old female for follow-up of fatigue. Labs show hemoglobin 9.1, MCV 72, ferritin 8, low iron saturation — iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy recently unremarkable; attributed to poor dietary intake. Started on ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with vitamin C. She smokes half pack daily for 50 years; counseled on nicotine dependence, agreed to nicotine patch and quit-line referral. Also has chronic pruritic, xerotic eczematous rash on lower legs and flexures — dermatitis; prescribed triamcinolone 0.1% ointment BID x 2 weeks and counseled on emollient use. Repeat CBC and ferritin in 8 weeks. Follow-up in 1 month.

Ward note. 72-year-old man with Alzheimer disease, diagnosed 4 years ago, now moderate stage, on donepezil and memantine; brought from a memory care facility with 2 days of abdominal pain, though he cannot clearly localize it. Staff report he stopped eating and is lying still with his right hip drawn up. Exam: temperature 100.9 F, guarding in the right lower quadrant; WBC 15.6. CT shows a dilated appendix with periappendiceal inflammation and early perforation changes. Assessment: acute appendicitis with early perforation superimposed on Alzheimer dementia. Plan: urgent laparoscopic appendectomy with IV piperacillin-tazobactam; family notified; donepezil and memantine continued postoperatively; delirium precautions given his dementia.

Hospital ward note. 76-year-old male admitted with acute ischemic stroke, right middle cerebral territory infarct on MRI with left-sided weakness and dysarthria; treated with aspirin and atorvastatin, physical therapy initiated. History of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35%), on furosemide, lisinopril, and carvedilol; mild bibasilar crackles, stable weight. He also has gastro-esophageal reflux disease managed with pantoprazole, complaining of heartburn when supine, and chronic plaque psoriasis on extensor surfaces and scalp, treated with topical clobetasol. Exam: left arm and leg strength 3/5, extensor erythematous scaly plaques with silvery scale. Plan: continue stroke workup and rehab, diuretic adjustment, reflux precautions, dermatology consult for psoriasis.

Primary care visit. 63-year-old male here for review of incidental liver enzyme elevation. Asymptomatic, no alcohol use. Exam unremarkable, BMI 30.1. Ultrasound shows increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with fatty infiltration of the liver; viral hepatitis serologies negative. Impression: nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Plan: weight reduction counseling, gradual exercise program, repeat liver panel in 3 months, avoid hepatotoxic medications, fasting glucose checked to screen for metabolic contributors.

Nephrology clinic, 30-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3 (eGFR 42, stable), followed for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 35% on last echocardiogram). Presents with a painful, swollen, erythematous first metatarsophalangeal joint over the past two days, classic for an acute gout flare. Medications: furosemide 40 mg daily, lisinopril, carvedilol; serum uric acid 9.1 mg/dL. Exam: JVP mildly elevated, bibasilar crackles, 1+ ankle edema; first MTP joint exquisitely tender and warm. Plan: colchicine 0.6 mg daily with renal dose adjustment, avoid NSAIDs given CKD, continue diuretic and HF regimen, recheck BMP and uric acid in 2 weeks, low-purine diet education.

ED. 87-year-old male brought in by family for 2 days of sore throat, odynophagia, and low-grade fever. Poor oral intake but no drooling or voice change.
